recares.name: ReCARES
intro: ReCARES collects donated medical equipment and supplies and gives them to people who need them.
Its three distribution sites serve San Francisco, Oakland and Marin.
Items such as walkers, wheelchairs and bathing aids can help recipients move around and manage daily care.
recares.recommendation: We include ReCARES among our top-ten research candidates because of its:
reasons: Low reported operating cost relative to the volume of equipment and supplies distributed.
Practical way to turn unused equipment into better mobility and self-care for someone facing an access barrier.
Established local distribution sites, volunteer participation and original annual financial filings.
reservations: Reported items and recipients are not a count of unique people gaining appropriately fitted, safely used equipment.
Health gains, unmet need and duration of use are modeled assumptions rather than measured ReCARES outcomes.
Existing financial assets, donated equipment and volunteer capacity must be reconciled with what additional cash would make possible.
cost: GiveBetter sees ReCARES as one of the most promising low-cost mechanisms in our Bay Area research: useful equipment already exists, and the organization helps move it to someone who needs it. FY2025 reported expense of $72,583 divided by reported activity floors of 45,000 items and 11,000 recipients is about $1.61 per item or $6.60 per reported recipient. These are historical accounting ratios, not the cost of purchasing a device or guaranteeing a new clinical benefit.

The reason this could matter is functional independence. Our revised central model assumes an appropriate mobility aid improves health-related quality of life by 0.03 for three months, equivalent to 0.0075 QALYs for a recipient who gains that benefit. This is an analyst assumption, not a measured effect per donated item; the model separately adjusts for alternative access, safe use, repeated recipients and expansion constraints.

After those adjustments and modeled harms, the central estimate is about $264,000 per better life (10 Bay health-plus-income-equivalent years), revised from $75,000 after checking clinical utility and duration. Net household savings are explicitly considered but receive a provisional zero central credit: many recipients would otherwise go without equipment, rather than buy it. A small positive purchasing-power case gives $262,000; an adverse acquisition-cost case gives $690,000. The signed weighted diagnostic is $294,000, not the ranking statistic.
recares.monitoring: ReCARES shares tax filings, distribution information and annual counts of recipients, items and volunteer hours. These establish substantial activity, but do not yet show deduplicated recipients, equipment fit, sustained use or outcomes compared with alternative access. Device-level follow-up and a priced expansion plan would make the estimate much more useful.
recares.qualitative: We value the combination of reuse, accessibility and practical help with daily life. ReCARES belongs on a donor's research shortlist, but the model does not yet establish a giving recommendation: we would first verify which additional safe services the money would fund.

hope-pacifica.name: HOPE Pacifica
intro: HOPE Pacifica supports local access to naloxone, the medication used to reverse an opioid overdose.
Its network includes distribution locations across Pacifica and nearby Bay Area communities.
It also provides overdose-prevention education and resources for families.
hope-pacifica.recommendation: We include HOPE Pacifica among our top-ten research candidates because of its:
reasons: Focus on a time-sensitive emergency where access to medication can save a life.
Local distribution network that could reach people not well served by other channels.
Potential to combine publicly supplied medication with relatively modest local stocking and outreach costs.
reservations: No original annual expense statement has been verified, so the operating budget in the model is assumed.
Stocking locations and cumulative distributions do not establish unique people protected or additional rescues.
Public medication and hardware provision may already cover some expansion; the recipient, funding need and extra activity require verification before a gift.
cost: GiveBetter considers local naloxone access an important mechanism to investigate, but does not currently recommend a HOPE donation on the available financial evidence. The central model assumes a $40,000 annual budget and 1,500 two-device packs distributed annually, equivalent to about $27 of organizational expense per pack. Neither figure is a verified HOPE budget or annual output, and the ratio is not the medication purchase price.

A pack helps only if usable naloxone reaches someone able to respond to an overdose that would otherwise go untreated. The model adjusts for readiness, repeated packs, people already covered by other services and what additional cash changes. It assumes a 0.002 reduction in annual mortality hazard during one year of additional coverage, then values subsequent survival over a finite horizon; it does not assign a saved life to each pack.

The current central estimate is about $932,000 per better life, revised from $555,000 after independently reviewing recipient reach. Per $1,000, the model combines .010705 Bay health years and .000028 one-off income-equivalent years. It assumes half of nonpurchasing holders reach a high-risk person or close witness, rather than the earlier 80%; this is a judgment informed by mixed public-access venues, not a survey. Five percent are assumed to avoid one $19 purchase and receive no added access-related health credit. Survival and additional funding remain important uncertainties.
hope-pacifica.monitoring: HOPE publishes location information and cumulative distribution totals. The latest reviewed pages identified nine sites, but did not establish annual packs, repeat recipients, stockouts or rescues caused by the service. The financial and outcome records needed to test the model remain incomplete.
hope-pacifica.qualitative: Community-led access and family support are credible reasons to investigate HOPE. They do not resolve the missing financial denominator or prove that a new donation adds protection beyond public provision. We retain it as a research candidate, not a current giving recommendation.

project-homeless-connect.name: Project Homeless Connect
intro: Project Homeless Connect helps people experiencing homelessness access health care and other practical services.
Its Core Senses work connects people with glasses, hearing care and dentures.
Staff and partners help with the appointments, fitting and follow-up needed to turn a referral into useful care.
project-homeless-connect.recommendation: We include Project Homeless Connect among our top-ten research candidates because of its:
reasons: Concrete route to improving vision, hearing and oral function rather than offering referrals alone.
Ability to address practical barriers that can persist even when a person has insurance.
Identifiable clinical partners and documented service events that make its delivery pathways inspectable.
reservations: Current project-level spending and additional completed-care capacity have not been publicly reconciled.
The model's treatment costs, funding allocations and completion assumptions are not verified prices for new services.
Health gains are transferred from studies in other settings, and patients served through partners must not be counted twice.
cost: GiveBetter sees completing corrective care as a promising way to improve daily life. Our model assumes $150 for a completed glasses episode, $1,500 for hearing care and $1,500 for dentures, including failed referrals and allocated delivery costs. These are analyst budgets, not provider quotes; simpler fundraising examples do not establish the full cost.

Better vision can make reading and navigating easier, hearing care can improve communication, and dentures can improve oral function. Independent review now uses a smaller glasses utility judgment of 0.02 and denture utility of 0.015, while hearing remains 0.02. Randomized vision-specific improvements and weak generic-utility evidence support a modest positive prior, not a measured PHC effect. Clinical use, alternatives and financing remain separate adjustments.

Keeping all modeled project-support costs gives a revised central estimate of about $1.50 million per better life, versus $774,000 before: 0.6182 Bay health QALYs plus 0.0473 income-equivalent years per illustrative $100,000. The income prior covers a small group gaining net resources from work and a disjoint group avoiding an actual purchase. Positive generic-health credit for the earning subgroup is conservatively excluded to limit overlap; clinical harms remain. Distinct health and income together give $1.37 million; zero resources give $1.46 million. The gross associated-resource diagnostic is $2.10 million, not net societal cost or a verified funding tranche.
project-homeless-connect.monitoring: PHC shares service descriptions, partner information and giving examples. Community Initiatives' filings establish its fiscal-sponsorship context, but do not supply a complete PHC program budget or patient-level cost-and-outcome dataset. Completed episodes, insurance contributions, follow-up and the number of additional patients funded would strengthen the analysis.
project-homeless-connect.qualitative: PHC's practical navigation role is a good fit for people whose access barriers are not solved by nominal coverage. We consider it a useful donor-shortlist candidate, conditional on current project accounts and a plan for additional completed care. Its hearing pathway overlaps with the Hearing and Speech Center assessment and should not be added to it as an independent benefit.

hearing-and-speech-center.name: Hearing and Speech Center
intro: The reviewed Hearing and Speech Center pathway provides hearing assessment and hearing aids to eligible adults.
It includes fitting, batteries, rehabilitation and follow-up rather than the device alone.
The pathway is described through its partnership with Project Homeless Connect.
hearing-and-speech-center.recommendation: We include this hearing-care pathway among our top-ten research candidates because of its:
reasons: Focus on fitted, supported hearing care that can improve communication.
External randomized evidence of improvement in hearing-related health utility.
Model that accounts for clinical time, follow-up and unsuccessful offers rather than pricing donated devices alone.
reservations: The historical recipient's tax-exempt status is unresolved; a current eligible recipient must be verified before a direct gift.
The assumed cost and additional treatment capacity are not supported by a current provider quote.
Study results may not transfer to local patients, sustained hearing-aid use is uncertain, and PHC overlap must be excluded.
cost: GiveBetter considers supported hearing care a plausible way to improve everyday functioning, but does not recommend a direct gift to this recipient until its status is resolved. We assume $1,500 per offered care package: $600 for clinical labor, $250 for refurbishment and molds, $250 for support, $200 for coordination and failed offers, and $200 for overhead and contingency. These are analyst assumptions; a separate donated-device resource allowance is not included in that donor price.

The revised clinical benchmark is 0.11 hearing-sensitive utility from an acoustic hearing-aid meta-analysis; generic EQ5D studies show much smaller changes. We assume 50% local transfer, 80% completion, a quarter-year delay and nine months of funded benefit, adjusted separately for persistence, survival and equivalent alternative care. These local inputs are judgments, not measured HSC outcomes.

At the assumed $1,500 cost, our independently reassessed central estimate is about $1.51 million per better life, revised from $1.25 million: 0.009715 health years plus 0.000233 income-equivalent years per offered course. We assume 10% of additional completed households gain net 2% annual resources during the funded window, with independent economic exposure. To limit generic-utility overlap, we conservatively exclude positive health credit proportionately for these earners; clinical harms remain. Keeping distinct communication and income benefits together gives $1.36 million. These are uncertain judgments, not measured earnings or confidence bounds.
hearing-and-speech-center.monitoring: The reviewed material describes a clinical pathway, but not current completed-course counts or local utility and earnings follow-up. Original FY2022/21/20 returns show historical whole expenses averaging $2.46M, not a current marginal fitting cost. Fresh September-cutoff IRS records still show revocation for the historical EIN, with no reinstatement date or exact Publication 78 match; a later successor or reinstatement remains unverified.
hearing-and-speech-center.qualitative: There is a credible clinical mechanism and a concrete local partnership. Administrative uncertainty about who can receive a donation is separate from whether the clinic provides useful care, and does not establish misconduct or closure. We keep the research while withholding a direct-gift recommendation.

compass-family-services.name: Compass Family Services
intro: Compass Family Services helps families facing homelessness and housing instability.
Its C-Rent program provides back-rent or move-in assistance alongside case management and problem-solving.
This estimate focuses on that prevention program rather than every service Compass provides.
compass-family-services.recommendation: We include Compass C-Rent among our top-ten research candidates because of its:
reasons: Direct response to a temporary cash gap that can put a family at risk of losing housing.
Audited program-specific spending, which gives a more concrete cost starting point than an assumed budget.
Related randomized evidence from nearby Santa Clara County supporting the potential of financial assistance to prevent homelessness.
reservations: Reported prevention families and audited C-Rent spending have not been fully reconciled to a unique-household denominator.
Household resources, net tenant capture and the independently assumed avoided-homelessness health effect are not measured Compass health or income effects.
A new donation needs to fund additional C-Rent assistance rather than replace already available funding or support a different program.
cost: GiveBetter sees targeted rent assistance as a promising way to resolve a housing crisis before it becomes more disruptive. FY2025 audited C-Rent expense of $2,008,658 divided by 207 reported prevention-classified families is about $9,704 per family: roughly $5,295 in housing assistance and $4,409 in other program expense. This is a historical accounting ratio, not a quote for an additional family kept housed.

Assistance can provide housing consumption, debt relief or freed household resources even without a change in recorded homelessness. Our central income allocation credits 80% of the $5,295 assistance ratio once, at an assumed quarter-year receipt and $50,000 annual household-resource baseline. Using Coefficient Giving’s logarithmic comparison, this is 0.040359 income-equivalent years per historical-equivalent case. The baseline and net tenant share are judgments; causal earnings are not separately credited.

We now independently estimate 0.000124 noncash health-proxy years per case from a 2% avoided-episode probability, three months of avoided exposure and a 0.025 adult-equivalent nonfinancial health gap. These are judgments, not measured clinical QALYs or a residual chosen to preserve the old total. With proportional shared-support allocation, the current comparison is about $2.83M per better life; omitting separately credited health gives about $2.84M. The original $1.35M inherited-envelope estimate and $485K per homelessness episode remain historical diagnostics, not the current combined-benefit estimate. Additional award capacity remains unverified.
compass-family-services.monitoring: Compass shares annual outcome reporting and audited program expenses. The reported 207 prevention classifications are useful activity evidence, but do not establish what would have happened without assistance. An applicant funnel, common follow-up, unique-household reconciliation and current unfunded demand would make the estimate stronger.
compass-family-services.qualitative: C-Rent is tangible and locally relevant: it can resolve a rent gap while staff support the family. Original recent audits and returns provide a more concrete cost basis than an assumed organization budget. Economic gains, broad housing wellbeing and recipient burdens need explicit separation; family spillovers may matter beyond what is quantified. A new gift still needs a confirmed additional allocation and capacity.

hamilton-families.name: Hamilton Families
intro: Hamilton Families helps families avoid homelessness and regain stable housing.
Its prevention assistance can cover back rent and future rent alongside income planning, referrals and case management.
The estimate here concerns prevention assistance, not an unrestricted donation across all Hamilton services.
hamilton-families.recommendation: We include Hamilton's prevention work among our top-ten research candidates because of its:
reasons: Concrete assistance package addressing arrears and the practical causes of housing loss.
Related randomized evidence for financial assistance in a nearby high-cost housing market.
Published housing outcomes that provide a starting point for more detailed evaluation.
reservations: The assumed cost per prevention family is not an observed Hamilton program cost.
Reported housing outcomes lack a comparison group and cannot all be attributed to Hamilton.
Health benefits and the additional assistance enabled by a new donation remain uncertain.
cost: GiveBetter sees a plausible opportunity in resolving a family's rent crisis before homelessness occurs. The model assumes $10,000 per assisted family, with an exploratory $5,000–$25,000 range, because Hamilton does not publish a prevention-only average award and delivery cost. That covers a package of financial assistance and support, not a guaranteed housing outcome.

The all-in $10,000 scenario includes an assumed $5,000 rent payment. At an 80% net tenant share and a $50,000 reference household-resource baseline, this produces 0.038197 income-equivalent years when valued once. Payment size, incidence and baseline are judgments, not measured Hamilton averages or recurring wages.

The current estimate is about $2.61M per ten combined income-equivalent and noncash health-proxy years, not measured clinical QALYs. We independently assume a 2% avoided-episode probability, three months of avoided exposure and a 0.025 nonfinancial health gap for one adult-equivalent: 0.000124 health-proxy years per award, added to the separately calculated 0.038197 resource-equivalent years. No inherited total minus cash is used. Cash-only gives about $2.62M. The earlier $1.39M inherited-envelope model and separate $500K homelessness-episode estimate remain historical diagnostics.
hamilton-families.monitoring: FY2025 reporting lists 127 families avoiding homelessness and 344 maintaining housing. Newly housed families are included in the latter measure and should not be added again. Program accounts, deduplicated applicants, comparable follow-up and a counterfactual would help distinguish service activity from additional results.
hamilton-families.qualitative: Hamilton offers an understandable response to a serious local problem, with possible family benefits beyond measured health. The main weakness for this comparison is the assumed prevention cost and transferred effect. We prioritize verification of those inputs before recommending a donation on cost-effectiveness grounds.

friends-of-the-urban-forest.name: Friends of the Urban Forest
intro: Friends of the Urban Forest plants and cares for San Francisco street trees.
It also installs sidewalk gardens and runs community and workforce programs.
Its establishment care helps new trees survive long enough to contribute shade and greenery.
friends-of-the-urban-forest.recommendation: We include Friends of the Urban Forest among our top-ten research candidates because of its:
reasons: Concrete planting and establishment care in San Francisco, with recent financial and activity records.
A plausible neighborhood-health mechanism supported by primary greening research, though local causal effects remain uncertain.
Temporary paid Green Crew work that may add household resources as well as planting capacity.
reservations: The mortality-to-health bridge rests on observational evidence and explicit causal, local and life-years judgments.
The incremental wage estimate uses cross-vintage program data and assumed counterfactual earnings, taxes and benefit offsets.
Existing city funding, replacement plantings and maintenance obligations leave donor-additional capacity unverified.
cost: GiveBetter is interested in street trees because shade and greenery can affect many nearby residents. FY2025 expense of $5,410,095 divided by 1,506 plantings is about $3,592 per planting equivalent, including all organizational programs and overhead. It is not a marginal tree quote.

Our current bridge applies Portland’s planted-tree mortality associations over fifteen years, with explicit causal and local-transfer judgments, rather than an unexplained QALY-per-surviving-tree-year scalar. We also count six months of modeled net additional Green Crew resources, not all payroll or an assumed permanent wage gain.

The conditional central estimate is about $6.6M per better life: ten combined modeled health and income-equivalent years. An illustrative $100,000 budget yields 0.147483 health years and 0.004085 income-equivalent years. The income-only estimate is much weaker; cautious and null-health cases can imply net harm. The former $942K weighted illustration is historical, not the current ranking.
friends-of-the-urban-forest.monitoring: FY2025 reports 1,506 plantings and eighteen workforce participants: ten Green Crew and eight New Roots. Their trees are already inside the planting total. Survival and net-new canopy cohorts, a donor-additional plan, and participant hours, counterfactual earnings and after-tax resources would improve the estimate.
friends-of-the-urban-forest.qualitative: Low-canopy targeting, community participation and workforce opportunities add reasons to care about the work, even where QALYs cannot capture them. Species choice, maintenance burden and potential harms also matter. We retain the organization as a promising systems-oriented research candidate while seeking better evidence on additional planting and health.

melp-ablecloset.name: MELP / AbleCloset
intro: MELP provides free reused medical equipment to people who need it.
AbleCloset also lends specialized equipment for children.
The service involves obtaining, repairing and matching equipment so that it can support mobility and daily care.
melp-ablecloset.recommendation: We include MELP / AbleCloset among our top-ten research candidates because of its:
reasons: Practical reuse-and-loan service that can reduce the cost of accessing useful equipment.
Specialized pediatric equipment pathway as well as adult mobility and bathing aids.
Public planning documents, financial reporting and current pickup arrangements that make operations inspectable.
reservations: The modeled client denominator is inferred from a planning document, not an observed count of unique recipients.
Existing reserves and public support make additional cash-funded expansion uncertain.
Appropriate fit, sustained use and health gains have not been measured locally, and evidence for some equipment pathways is mixed.
cost: GiveBetter sees promise in reusing equipment to improve mobility and daily care without requiring every household to buy a new device. Our conditional central estimate is about $3.6M per better life in the Bay Area, combining health-access gains and net household resource savings. Planned organization expense divided by inferred planning activity is about $49 per client-equivalent, not an observed additional-loan price.

For someone who otherwise lacks timely equivalent equipment, an adult mobility aid may improve walking and independence. The central clinical judgment is a 0.03 utility improvement over an incremental 0.125-year bridge, before adjustments for unmet access, safe use and donor additionality. Pediatric benefit is a separate weaker assumption; administrative loan length does not establish clinical exposure.

For a disjoint group who would buy or rent equivalent equipment anyway, the model credits one-off net savings rather than additional equipment-access health. It assumes $40/$25/$100/$20 of net savings across mobility, bathing, pediatric and supply needs. Per illustrative donor budget, 0.02478918 health years plus 0.00411209 income-equivalent years give 0.02745621 Bay-attributed combined years. These resource and clinical assumptions are not locally measured.
melp-ablecloset.monitoring: The organization shares equipment activity, pickup information and planning targets, including a reported 3,874 items over a recent twelve-month period. Items are not unique clients, and planned activity is not completed service. A deduplicated record of equipment type, actual use and alternative access would help test the model.
melp-ablecloset.qualitative: Reuse and specialized pediatric lending address concrete needs with modest cash expenditure per planning episode. Current operations and original financial returns make the service inspectable. Donor-triggered capacity, recipient alternatives and net savings still need verification before treating the modeled ratio as an actionable funding opportunity.

code-tenderloin.name: Code Tenderloin
intro: Code Tenderloin provides community-based support in San Francisco, including employment, youth and reentry services.
Its ambassador work includes peer contact and help during emergencies.
Our estimate combines additional timely overdose response with net resources from paid peer work, retaining the cost of other activities.
code-tenderloin.recommendation: We include Code Tenderloin among our top-ten research candidates because of its:
reasons: Local peer relationships that may reach people conventional services miss.
Paid on-the-job training that may improve workers’ resources relative to their alternatives.
A potentially important role in timely overdose response, alongside broader community support.
reservations: The complete worker-hour cost, paid tenure, alternative earnings and allocation of new funding are assumptions.
Additional high-risk reach and the change in emergency outcomes have not been measured.
Current accounts, public funding and historical sponsor arrangements need reconciliation before estimating extra capacity.
cost: GiveBetter sees a potentially valuable mechanism in having a trusted person nearby who can recognize and respond to an overdose. An advertised ambassador wage of about $27 an hour anchors our assumed $60 complete worker-hour cost. Six worker-hours per offered person-year give an assumed $360 delivery package; after 50% funding additionality, branch spending is about $720 per additional package, before allocating general organizational costs.

The model asks whether those contacts close a rescue gap beyond existing services. It assumes peers close 10% of the remaining gap with 90% effectiveness, reducing modeled overdose hazard by 9%. It values extra survival once over a finite ten-year horizon rather than awarding a new lifetime for each reported reversal.

With 25% of additional support allocated to peer work, our central estimate is about $1.72 million per better life in the Bay Area: ten combined health and income-equivalent years. The same additional paid hours support both response and workers’ household resources. We assume an $8.60 hourly resource gain after taxes, alternative pay, lost benefits and work costs, and a one-year paid-work window; negative resource changes remain possible. This improves the earlier health-only estimate modestly, rather than treating all payroll or reported job placements as extra welfare.
code-tenderloin.monitoring: Current program descriptions and the advertised $27 hourly ambassador wage support ongoing activity. Three original sponsor returns identify historical Code program spending, but not current standalone finances. Worker-hour logs, distinct people reached, emergency outcomes, paid tenure and net alternative resources would allow the estimate to be calibrated to actual additional activity.
code-tenderloin.qualitative: Trusted relationships, employment and reentry support can have value beyond the health pathways quantified here. The emergency-response mechanism deserves attention, but we would not infer cost-effectiveness from contact or reversal counts alone. Current funding and patient overlap with other providers are important next checks.

san-francisco-aids-foundation.name: San Francisco AIDS Foundation
intro: San Francisco AIDS Foundation provides HIV prevention and care, sexual health services and community support.
Its work includes overdose prevention and access to PrEP, medication that reduces the risk of acquiring HIV.
General donations support this broader range of services rather than only naloxone distribution.
san-francisco-aids-foundation.recommendation: We include San Francisco AIDS Foundation among our top-ten research candidates because of its:
reasons: Established clinical and community services with current audited financial reporting.
Concrete prevention mechanisms, including timely overdose response and effective HIV prophylaxis.
Ability to address practical access barriers alongside medical care and community support.
reservations: The allocation of additional donations and delivery prices in our model are assumptions, not verified marginal budgets.
Added access beyond public coverage, partner services and existing rescue networks has not been measured.
Net patient resources, including avoided bills and extra access costs, are not identified; much of the broader portfolio remains unquantified.
cost: GiveBetter is interested in extending effective prevention to people who otherwise miss it. The model assumes $300 per overdose-response offer and $700 per PrEP offer, including branch delivery and follow-up. After assumptions about replacing existing funding, branch spending is about $750 per additional overdose offer and $2,333 per additional PrEP offer, before other organizational costs and overlap adjustments; these are analyst budgets, not provider quotes.

Overdose response can extend survival when it changes an otherwise untreated emergency, while PrEP can add time living without HIV. The model compares each with the care people would otherwise receive, follows finite health trajectories and avoids double-counting overlapping participants. It does not treat each naloxone dose or reported reversal as a separate life saved.

The central estimate is about $1.93 million per better life in the Bay Area, or $2.02 million for San Francisco benefits alone, per ten combined health and income-equivalent years. It retains the finite clinical estimate and explicitly sets unidentified net patient resources to zero centrally, with positive and negative economic scenarios. This is not evidence that housing or benefits counseling has no value. Actual avoided bills must be net of fees, travel, lost work and other assistance; retail drug prices and public payments are not household income.
san-francisco-aids-foundation.monitoring: SFAF shares audited accounts, annual reporting and service information. These establish the scale and breadth of its work, but doses, contacts and reversals are not a patient-linked counterfactual evaluation. The most useful additional information would connect incremental funding with unique people gaining sustained protection beyond existing access.
san-francisco-aids-foundation.qualitative: Established delivery, clinical expertise and community relationships make SFAF a credible organization for a donor to investigate. HIV care, housing and behavioral-health support may add benefits not captured by our calculation. Our positive view of the organization is therefore distinct from confidence in any particular marginal QALY estimate.
